slots.name: Bulkhead between fuel and oxidizer
slots.role: How the two propellants are kept apart.

options.name: Separate domes
options.note: Two tanks, two domes, a short section between them. Simple and safe.
cons: Heavier: two domes and a gap
options.real: Delta II, Atlas V

options.name: Common bulkhead
options.note: One insulated wall shared by both propellants. Saves a dome and a metre of skin; the hardest thing to build in the tank.
cons: A leak mixes fuel and oxidizer
options.real: Saturn S-II, Falcon 9, Starship

slots.name: Wall stiffening
slots.role: How the tank wall is stiffened so it does not buckle.

options.name: Integral stiffeners, as designed
options.note: Ribs and ring frames machined or milled into the wall, the standard way. Their mass and price are already in the tank's numbers.
options.real: Saturn V S-IC tanks (machined T-stiffeners in 2219 aluminium); Shuttle External Tank hydrogen barrels (skin, stringers and frames)

options.name: Isogrid
options.note: The wall is machined into a web of equilateral triangles: equally stiff in every direction, so equipment can bolt anywhere. Most of the thick plate ends up as chips.
options.real: Delta II, Atlas V and Delta IV cores; H-IIA (machined on the inside); NASA Isogrid Design Handbook CR-124075 (1973)

options.name: Orthogrid
options.note: Ribs running along and around the tank make square pockets: simpler to machine and weld into big panels than triangles, a little less stiff.
options.real: SLS core stage (2219 aluminium, friction-stir welded); Vulcan and New Glenn tanks

options.name: Waffle grid
options.note: Square pockets milled out of thick plate: stiff against twisting as well as squashing.
options.real: Saturn S-IVB (19 mm 2014 plate milled into pockets about 76 mm across); Energia hydrogen tank (about 3,000 cells per section from 45 mm stock); Zenit

slots.name: Pressurisation
slots.role: What fills the space as propellant drains.

options.name: Helium bottles inside
options.note: Cold helium bottles sit inside the oxygen tank, where they stay dense. Proven; the bottles are a hazard.
options.real: Falcon 9, Delta II

options.name: Autogenous (hot propellant gas)
options.note: A little propellant is heated by the engine and piped back as gas. No helium at all.
pros: No helium to run out of
cons: Only works once the engine runs
options.real: Starship, Shuttle ET

options.name: Heated helium
options.note: Helium from cold bottles is warmed in a heat exchanger on the engine before it enters the tank. Warm gas fills more volume, so fewer bottles do the job.
cons: One more heat exchanger on the engine
options.real: Falcon 9 (heated helium), Saturn V S-IC fuel tank

options.name: Nitrogen gas
options.note: Plain nitrogen instead of helium: cheap and easy to get, but seven times heavier per litre, and useless with hydrogen, which would freeze it solid.
options.real: Delta II first stage; Soyuz boils liquid nitrogen to pressurise its tanks

slots.name: Slosh baffles
slots.role: Rings inside the tank that stop the propellant sloshing.

options.name: Ring baffles
options.note: Rings welded inside the wall break up the waves when the ship turns.
options.real: Every crewed launcher

options.name: No baffles
options.note: Save the mass and hope. Sloshing propellant knocked Falcon 1 flight 2 into a spin.
options.real: Falcon 1 flight 2 (2007)

options.name: Ring baffles and anti-vortex vanes
options.note: As well as the rings, crossed vanes over each outlet stop the draining propellant swirling into a whirlpool, which would suck gas into the pump.
options.real: Saturn V S-IC LOX outlets; every modern stage

options.name: Baffles and screen channels
options.note: As well as the rings, fine mesh channels and vanes at the outlet hold liquid there by surface tension, so the engine gets liquid even in weightlessness.
pros: Liquid at the outlet in weightlessness
options.real: Propellant management devices (vanes, sponges and screen channels) in spacecraft propellant tanks (NASA NTRS 20110000503)

slots.name: Insulation
slots.role: What keeps cold propellant from boiling off.

options.name: Bare metal
options.note: Fine for kerosene; cryogenic propellant boils off in the hours on the pad.
options.real: Falcon 9 (kerosene stage)

options.name: Spray-on foam
options.note: The orange foam of the Shuttle tank. Keeps hydrogen and oxygen liquid for hours; a piece of it struck Columbia.
options.real: Shuttle External Tank, SLS

options.name: Multilayer blankets
options.note: Gold foil layers for the long cruise: the only insulation that works in vacuum for weeks.
options.real: Centaur, lunar landers

options.name: Bare aluminium, anodised copper finish
options.note: No foam: the bare metal gets anodised and conversion coatings against corrosion, which give it a copper-tan colour. Enough for kerosene; cryogenic oxygen boils off a little faster than under foam.
pros: Protects the bare metal from corrosion: reliability +0.05 %
options.real: Atlas V common core booster (ULA): bare isogrid aluminium with no foam (the user's guide lists foam only on Centaur); ULA's chief executive put the copper colour down to its anodise and conversion coatings

slots.name: Feed lines
slots.role: The pipes that carry propellant from the tank to the engine.

options.name: Single feed line
options.note: One big pipe per propellant.
cons: One valve failure stops the engine
options.real: Most stages

options.name: Redundant feed lines
options.note: Two pipes and two valves per propellant, so one can fail.
options.real: Saturn V S-IC (five feed lines)

options.name: Through-tank tunnel
options.note: The upper tank's line drops straight down through the middle of the lower tank inside an insulated tunnel: no bends, the fastest flow, but one more hole in every dome.
options.real: Saturn V S-IC (five LOX tunnels through the fuel tank), Falcon 9 LOX transfer tube, Super Heavy methane downcomer

options.name: Feed line with a pogo accumulator
options.note: A gas-filled pocket on the oxygen line soaks up pressure waves, so the engine and the pipe cannot set each other shaking up and down (pogo).
options.real: Titan II for Gemini (oxidizer standpipes and a fuel accumulator, 1963–64); Saturn V S-II centre-engine LOX accumulator from Apollo 14, after pogo shut down the Apollo 13 centre engine

slots.name: Flight computer
slots.role: The launcher's guidance computer.

options.name: Dual string
options.note: Two computers, each able to fly alone.
options.real: Delta II RIFCA

options.name: Triple voting
options.note: Three computers vote.
options.real: Ariane 5, Falcon 9

slots.name: Inertial measurement unit
slots.role: The gyroscopes and accelerometers that sense every turn and push.

options.name: Ring-laser gyros
options.note: Light beams racing around a triangle of mirrors. The launcher standard.
options.real: Delta II, Atlas V

options.name: Fibre-optic gyros
options.note: The same trick in a coil of fibre: lighter, no moving parts.
options.real: Falcon 9, many satellites

options.name: MEMS chips
options.note: Phone-grade silicon gyros, a hundred of them averaged.
options.real: Cubesats, Electron

options.name: Inertial reference, reused software
options.note: A laser-gyro inertial reference running software carried over from an older rocket, never tested against this rocket's own flight.
options.real: Ariane 5 flight 501 (4 June 1996): the inertial reference system ran software reused from Ariane 4; converting a 64-bit number to 16 bits overflowed 36.7 s after main-engine ignition, about 30 s into the flight

slots.name: Telemetry & range safety
slots.role: The radios that report home and listen for the destruct command.

options.name: Single transmitter
options.note: One S-band transmitter and one command receiver.
cons: One failure and the range loses the vehicle
options.real: Small launchers

options.name: Dual, cross-strapped
options.note: Two of everything, either able to serve the whole ring.
options.real: Delta II, Atlas V

slots.name: Navigation aids
slots.role: What corrects the gyros as they slowly drift.

options.name: Inertial only
options.note: The gyros and accelerometers alone. They drift a little every minute and nothing corrects them.
cons: Drift adds up on a long flight
options.real: Saturn V (ST-124-M platform), Delta II

options.name: GPS-aided inertial
options.note: A GPS receiver checks the position every second during the climb and trims the drift away.
options.real: Falcon 9, Atlas V, Electron

options.name: Star-tracker aided
options.note: A small camera recognises the stars and resets the gyros. It works anywhere, including on the way to Mars.
options.real: Trident missiles (stellar-inertial), deep-space probes

slots.name: Flight termination
slots.role: What ends the flight safely if the vehicle strays off course.

options.name: Commanded destruct
options.note: A range safety officer on the ground watches the track and sends the destruct command if the vehicle strays. A radio link and a person in the loop.
cons: Needs the radio link to the ground
options.real: Saturn V, Space Shuttle, Delta II

options.name: Autonomous flight termination (AFTS)
options.note: The vehicle's own computers check the track against the safety rules and decide for themselves. No radio link to lose, no needless destruct when the link drops.
options.real: Falcon 9 (first used 2017), Electron

slots.name: Cooling
slots.role: How the electronics get rid of their heat.

options.name: Ground air and heat sinks, as designed
options.note: Cool air blows in through the umbilical until lift-off; in flight the boxes soak their heat into their mounts. Enough for a climb that lasts minutes.
cons: The boxes warm up on a long flight
options.real: Saturn V Instrument Unit: pre-launch air-conditioning duct beside its umbilical

options.name: Cold plates and a sublimator
options.note: The boxes sit on plates with a methanol-water coolant running through them; a sublimator boils water off into space to dump the heat. The electronics stay at room temperature for hours.
pros: Steady temperature on a long flight
options.real: Saturn V Instrument Unit: up to 16 cold plates of at least 420 W each, 60/40 methanol-water at 15 °C, and a water sublimator

slots.name: Solar cells
slots.role: Which kind of cell covers the panel.

options.name: Silicon
options.note: 20 % efficient. Cheap and tough.
options.real: ISS original arrays

options.name: Triple-junction GaAs
options.note: Three layers, each catching a different colour: 30 %+ efficient.
options.real: Every modern spacecraft

slots.name: Array drive
slots.role: Whether the panel turns to follow the Sun.

options.name: Fixed
options.note: Bolted to the hull. Power depends on where the ship points.

options.name: Sun-tracking drive
options.note: A motor and slip rings keep the panel facing the Sun.
cons: A motor that must not jam
options.real: ISS SARJ, Dawn

slots.name: Common bulkhead
slots.role: The single wall shared by the two propellants.

options.name: Common bulkhead, as designed
options.note: The single shared dome this tank was designed with, between the kerosene or methane and the oxygen. Its mass and price are already in the tank's numbers.
pros: Saves a dome and the intertank
cons: A leak mixes fuel and oxidizer
options.real: Falcon 9, Starship and Super Heavy, Electron

options.name: Extra-insulated honeycomb sandwich
options.note: Two skins glued to a thicker honeycomb core. Each liquid stays at its own temperature, so neither boils nor freezes the other, and the bond is inspected cell by cell.
options.real: Saturn V S-II (phenolic honeycomb, saved 3.6 t), Centaur III (fibreglass honeycomb)

options.name: Thin-gauge, chemically milled
options.note: Acid baths eat the metal away wherever the loads are low. Lighter, with less margin left for a bad day.
options.real: Chemical milling, used on rocket tank skins and dome gores since the Saturn stages

slots.role: What stops the thin steel from crumpling when the tank is not full of propellant.

options.name: Always pressurised, crew on watch
options.note: From the factory to lift-off the tank is never without gas inside: nitrogen on the ground, propellant pressure in flight. A gauge and a crew watch it around the clock.

options.name: Thinner skin

slots.name: Construction
slots.role: How the shell is made stiff enough to carry the stack above it.

options.name: Skin and stringers
options.note: Thin aluminium skin riveted to long stiffeners (stringers) and ring frames: the aircraft way. Easy to inspect and repair.
options.real: Shuttle External Tank intertank, Falcon 9 fuel tank

options.name: Isogrid
options.note: Thick plate machined into a web of equilateral triangles. Equally stiff in every direction, so equipment can bolt to any node. Most of the metal ends up as chips on the floor.
options.real: Delta II first stage (isogrid aluminium panels), Atlas V booster

options.name: Orthogrid
options.note: The same idea with a square grid: simpler to machine and to weld into big panels, a little less efficient than triangles.
options.real: SLS core stage, Delta IV common booster core

options.name: Corrugated skin
options.note: Skin pressed into ridges like a tin roof, with stringers on the outside. Very stiff against squashing and cheap to make; a little heavier and draggier.
options.real: Saturn V S-IC forward skirt, thrust structure and interstage (7075 aluminium)

options.name: Honeycomb sandwich
options.note: Two thin skins bonded to a honeycomb core and baked in an autoclave: very stiff for its weight. The skins are whatever material you chose: aluminium, or carbon fibre as on the Falcon 9 interstage. A dent can hide a broken core under an intact skin.
options.real: Falcon 9 interstage (carbon skins on aluminium honeycomb), Ariane payload adapters, most fairings

slots.name: Joints
slots.role: How the panels are joined to each other.

options.name: Riveted and bolted
options.note: Panels riveted together, flanges bolted to the next section. Every joint can be inspected and redone.
options.real: Saturn V, Shuttle External Tank intertank

options.name: Friction-stir welded
options.note: A spinning tool stirs the two edges together without melting them: welds nearly as strong as the plate itself and no rivets at all.
options.real: Falcon 9, SLS core stage, Shuttle super-lightweight tank

options.name: Adhesive-bonded
options.note: Glued joints: smooth, light and cheap, but a bond that lets go looks exactly like one that holds.
options.real: Composite interstages and fairings

slots.name: Insulation
slots.role: What keeps liquid hydrogen from boiling away.

options.name: Spray-on foam, as designed
options.note: The orange foam of the Shuttle tank, sprayed on and trimmed by hand. Without it, hydrogen at −253 °C boils off in minutes and air freezes onto the skin. Its mass and price are already in the tank's numbers.

cons: Can shed pieces on ascent: a piece struck Columbia
options.real: Shuttle External Tank, SLS core stage, Delta IV

options.name: Bare metal
options.note: Leave the foam off. Lighter and cheaper, but the hydrogen boils away fast, ice builds on the skin, and the engines start on warmer, thinner propellant.
cons: Ice and boil-off on the pad
options.real: Only short-lived test tanks

options.name: Foam under multilayer blankets
options.note: Foam for the pad and the climb, gold foil blankets on top for the long cruise: in vacuum the blankets stop the Sun's heat almost completely.
pros: Weeks in space with little boil-off
options.real: Long-coast hydrogen upper stages and NASA cryogenic storage tests

options.name: Foam inside the tank
options.note: Foam tiles reinforced with glass-fibre threads are glued to the inside of the wall and lined with cloth. The outer wall stays warm and dry, and nothing can break off into the airflow.
options.real: Saturn S-IVB: about 4,300 tiles of polyurethane foam reinforced by glass-fibre threads in three directions, lined with resin-soaked glass cloth

options.name: Spray-on foam, painted white
options.note: White paint over the foam reflects sunlight, so less hydrogen boils off on a long coast. The paint is extra mass.
options.real: Shuttle External Tanks of STS-1 and STS-2 (paint dropped afterwards, saving about 272 kg); H-IIA second-stage LH2 tank painted white for long coasts

options.name: Sprayed and bonded foam, tan

options.name: Extra-insulated honeycomb sandwich
options.note: Two skins glued to a thicker honeycomb core. Each liquid stays at its own temperature, so neither boils nor freezes the other, and the bond is inspected cell by cell.
options.real: Thicker cores were studied for long-coast hydrogen stages; Centaur III uses fibreglass honeycomb

options.name: Thin-gauge, chemically milled
options.note: Acid baths eat the metal away wherever the loads are low. Lighter, with less margin left for a bad day.
options.real: Chemical milling, used on rocket tank skins and dome gores since the Saturn stages

slots.name: Wall stiffening
slots.role: How the tank wall is stiffened so it does not buckle.

options.name: Integral stiffeners, as designed
options.note: Ribs and ring frames machined or milled into the wall, the standard way. Their mass and price are already in the tank's numbers.
options.real: Saturn V S-IC tanks (machined T-stiffeners in 2219 aluminium); Shuttle External Tank hydrogen barrels (skin, stringers and frames)

options.name: Isogrid
options.note: The wall is machined into a web of equilateral triangles: equally stiff in every direction, so equipment can bolt anywhere. Most of the thick plate ends up as chips.
options.real: Delta II, Atlas V and Delta IV cores; H-IIA (machined on the inside); NASA Isogrid Design Handbook CR-124075 (1973)

options.name: Orthogrid
options.note: Ribs running along and around the tank make square pockets: simpler to machine and weld into big panels than triangles, a little less stiff.
options.real: SLS core stage (2219 aluminium, friction-stir welded); Vulcan and New Glenn tanks

options.name: Waffle grid
options.note: Square pockets milled out of thick plate: stiff against twisting as well as squashing.
options.real: Saturn S-IVB (19 mm 2014 plate milled into pockets about 76 mm across); Energia hydrogen tank (about 3,000 cells per section from 45 mm stock); Zenit

slots.name: Pressurisation
slots.role: What fills the space as propellant drains.

options.name: Helium bottles inside
options.note: Cold helium bottles sit inside the oxygen tank, where they stay dense. Proven; the bottles are a hazard.
options.real: Falcon 9, Delta II

options.name: Autogenous (hot propellant gas)
options.note: A little propellant is heated by the engine and piped back as gas. No helium at all.
pros: No helium to run out of
cons: Only works once the engine runs
options.real: Starship, Shuttle ET

options.name: Heated helium
options.note: Helium from cold bottles is warmed in a heat exchanger on the engine before it enters the tank. Warm gas fills more volume, so fewer bottles do the job.
cons: One more heat exchanger on the engine
options.real: Falcon 9 (heated helium), Saturn V S-IC fuel tank

options.name: Cold helium stored in the hydrogen
options.note: The helium bottles sit in the liquid hydrogen, where the cold packs the gas tight; a heater warms it on its way into the tanks.
cons: One more heater that must work
options.real: Saturn S-IVB: helium spheres inside the LH2 tank, warmed by heat exchangers and an O2/H2 burner for restarts

slots.name: Slosh baffles
slots.role: Rings inside the tank that stop the propellant sloshing.

options.name: Ring baffles
options.note: Rings welded inside the wall break up the waves when the ship turns.
options.real: Every crewed launcher

options.name: No baffles
options.note: Save the mass and hope. Sloshing propellant knocked Falcon 1 flight 2 into a spin.
options.real: Falcon 1 flight 2 (2007)

options.name: Ring baffles and anti-vortex vanes
options.note: As well as the rings, crossed vanes over each outlet stop the draining propellant swirling into a whirlpool, which would suck gas into the pump.
options.real: Saturn V S-IC LOX outlets; every modern stage

options.name: Baffles and screen channels
options.note: As well as the rings, fine mesh channels and vanes at the outlet hold liquid there by surface tension, so the engine gets liquid even in weightlessness.
pros: Liquid at the outlet in weightlessness
options.real: Propellant management devices (vanes, sponges and screen channels) in spacecraft propellant tanks (NASA NTRS 20110000503)

slots.name: Insulation
slots.role: What keeps liquid hydrogen from boiling away.

options.name: Spray-on foam, as designed
options.note: The orange foam of the Shuttle tank, sprayed on and trimmed by hand. Without it, hydrogen at −253 °C boils off in minutes and air freezes onto the skin. Its mass and price are already in the tank's numbers.
pros: Hydrogen stays liquid on the pad and in the climb
cons: Can shed pieces on ascent: a piece struck Columbia
options.real: Shuttle External Tank, SLS core stage, Delta IV

options.name: Bare metal
options.note: Leave the foam off. Lighter and cheaper, but the hydrogen boils away fast, ice builds on the skin, and the engines start on warmer, thinner propellant.
cons: Ice and boil-off on the pad
options.real: Only short-lived test tanks

options.name: Foam under multilayer blankets
options.note: Foam for the pad and the climb, gold foil blankets on top for the long cruise: in vacuum the blankets stop the Sun's heat almost completely.
pros: Weeks in space with little boil-off
options.real: Long-coast hydrogen upper stages and NASA cryogenic storage tests

options.name: Foam inside the tank
options.note: Foam tiles reinforced with glass-fibre threads are glued to the inside of the wall and lined with cloth. The outer wall stays warm and dry, and nothing can break off into the airflow.
options.real: Saturn S-IVB: about 4,300 tiles of polyurethane foam reinforced by glass-fibre threads in three directions, lined with resin-soaked glass cloth

options.name: Spray-on foam, painted white
options.note: White paint over the foam reflects sunlight, so less hydrogen boils off on a long coast. The paint is extra mass.
options.real: Shuttle External Tanks of STS-1 and STS-2 (paint dropped afterwards, saving about 272 kg); H-IIA second-stage LH2 tank painted white for long coasts

slots.name: Feed lines
slots.role: The pipes that carry propellant from the tank to the engine.

options.name: Single feed line
options.note: One big pipe per propellant.
cons: One valve failure stops the engine
options.real: Most stages

options.name: Redundant feed lines
options.note: Two pipes and two valves per propellant, so one can fail.
options.real: Saturn V S-IC (five feed lines)

options.name: Through-tank tunnel
options.note: The upper tank's line drops straight down through the middle of the lower tank inside an insulated tunnel: no bends, the fastest flow, but one more hole in every dome.
options.real: Saturn V S-IC (five LOX tunnels through the fuel tank), Falcon 9 LOX transfer tube, Super Heavy methane downcomer

options.name: Feed line with a pogo accumulator
options.note: A gas-filled pocket on the oxygen line soaks up pressure waves, so the engine and the pipe cannot set each other shaking up and down (pogo).
options.real: Titan II for Gemini (oxidizer standpipes and a fuel accumulator, 1963–64); Saturn V S-II centre-engine LOX accumulator from Apollo 14, after pogo shut down the Apollo 13 centre engine

slots.role: What keeps cold propellant from boiling off.

options.name: Bare metal
options.note: Fine for kerosene; cryogenic propellant boils off in the hours on the pad.
options.real: Falcon 9 (kerosene stage)

options.name: Spray-on foam
options.note: The orange foam of the Shuttle tank. Keeps hydrogen and oxygen liquid for hours; a piece of it struck Columbia.

options.name: Multilayer blankets
options.note: Gold foil layers for the long cruise: the only insulation that works in vacuum for weeks.

slots.name: Heat shield on the dome below
slots.role: What protects the dome under the joint from the flame of the engine that lights inside it.

options.name: Heat-resistant cover, as designed
options.note: A cover over the dome below takes the flame of the engine that lights inside the joint. Its mass and price are already in the numbers.
cons: Mass that does no other work
options.real: Soyuz: a cone-shaped, titanium-covered deflector over the Block A instrument bay (RussianSpaceWeb)

options.name: No shield
options.note: Leave the cover off and trust the dome.
options.real: Gemini 10 (1966): the spent first-stage oxidizer tank ruptured just after staging, possibly hit by the second-stage exhaust
